intro: Paste the inventory — decision points, the systems touching each with procurement or shadow-stack origin noted, and the four-question test applied to your three highest-stakes review layers — followed by the 250–350 word write-up including your position on this module's claim. Resubmission is free and unlimited — the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext:
You are grading a learner submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, Defensible by Design. Module 2 applied activity, 'The AEDT inventory': every decision point in the employment lifecycle where an outcome is determined, narrowed, ordered or scored; the systems touching each, with what it is, what decision it touches, the vendor, whether it arrived through PROCUREMENT or as a FEATURE, and whether anyone owns it; and the four-question test (information, time, authority, incentive) applied to the review layer on the three highest-stakes systems, answered with facts rather than intentions.

The shadow-stack distinction is the module's central finding and should be scored hard. An inventory where every system arrived through procurement has almost certainly listed the procurement register rather than searched for capability — feature-delivered AI is the fastest-growing category, and its absence from a submission usually means the five discovery questions were not run. Look specifically for evidence of the default-sort check and the built-it-ourselves question.

Step 3 must be answered with facts: how many items, in how many minutes, seeing what, able to override how, with what consequence. 'Our recruiters review everything carefully' is an intention. 'Don't know, and the person who would know is X' is a strong answer and should score at the top — this rubric rewards accurate uncertainty over confident assertion throughout.

Do not require legal conclusions. This module is counsel-gated and the learner is not counsel.

Watch for two specific omissions worth naming in feedback: sourcing (who sees the posting at all, which shapes the applicant pool before anyone applies) and selection for reduction (usually a spreadsheet, usually the highest-stakes scoring instrument in the organization, almost never on an inventory).

This track scores the delta rather than the score. Grade the learner's ACCOUNT of the gap between systems predicted and systems found — direction, size, and what it reveals. NEVER grade prediction accuracy. Finding far more than predicted is the module working as designed.

opening.label: Predicted — distinct systems touching an employment decision in your organization
opening.hint: Sourcing through selection for reduction. Before you go looking.

calibration.label: Found — how many the inventory turned up
calibration.hint: Including feature-delivered capability and anything built in-house.

dimensions.name: Decision points are mapped before systems
dimensions.criteria: The lifecycle walked and outcome-determining points named, rather than a software list retrofitted to decisions. Sourcing and selection for reduction are the two most commonly missed; their absence should be named in feedback. A submission that begins with the ATS and works outward has inherited the blind spot this method exists to avoid.

dimensions.name: The shadow stack is actually searched for
dimensions.criteria: Evidence the five discovery questions were run — particularly the default-sort check and the built-it-ourselves question — with each system marked as procured or feature-delivered. An inventory in which everything arrived through procurement is the failure mode: it has listed the purchase register. In-house spreadsheets, saved prompts and scripts count and should appear.

dimensions.name: The review test is answered with facts
dimensions.criteria: Item counts, minutes, what the reviewer can see, whether overriding needs approval, and what happens to a reviewer who overrides and is wrong. Intentions ('we review carefully') are not answers. 'Don't know, and X would know' scores at the top — accurate uncertainty beats confident assertion, and naming who holds the answer is the actionable part.

dimensions.name: Ownership and origin are recorded
dimensions.criteria: For each system: who owns it, or an explicit 'nobody'. Feature-delivered capability frequently has no owner at all, and recording that is more valuable than assigning a plausible name. Systems enabled by default — where the deployment decision was effectively made by a vendor's product team — should be flagged as such where identifiable.

dimensions.name: The position engages the discoverability counter
dimensions.criteria: A committed position on the claim, engaging the strongest case against it: that a complete inventory is unachievable and chasing it spends governance capacity on discovery rather than control, and — sharper — that the inventory is itself discoverable, a self-funded roadmap for opposing counsel, so the prudent move might be to find the machines and write down very little. Engaging the discoverability version specifically is what separates a strong submission, since Module 3 answers it with a mechanism. Plus the one system they didn't know existed, or an honest account of why there wasn't one.
